--- title: "Observations and features" description: "The parts of a data table and their other names, and why a table's row count is not the number of independent observations it holds." order: 2 categories: [data-preparation, marine-data] --- ## Every method learns from a table Every method in this course learns from a table of data. This page names the parts of that table, so later pages can use the words freely, and shows why a table of several hundred rows can hold far fewer independent observations. How many you really have decides how far you can trust any score a model gets. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the data on this page The coastal survey used here is **simulated**, not a real survey. That is deliberate: because we wrote the generating process (`R/make-example-data.R`), we know the true relationships and can show whether a model recovers them. No real survey is being misrepresented, and the figures are not results about any real species. See `data/README.md` for what is built into it. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the Python tabs Most code blocks on this page have an **R** and a **Python** tab, and picking one switches the whole page. Both run when the site is built, and each tab shows its own output. The Python tab is the scikit-learn equivalent of the R; the figures come from R throughout, and a few steps with no scikit-learn counterpart have no Python tab, which is itself worth noticing. Expect the **numbers to differ slightly** where randomness is involved: R and Python draw their random splits from different generators, so the split is not the same one. The conclusions are. ::: ## Rows are observations and columns are features A data table has one **observation** in each row: one thing that was measured, such as one water sample. Each column records one property of it. The columns a model learns from are its **features**, which this course also calls its **inputs**. The column it learns to predict is the **outcome**. When the outcome is a category, such as present or absent, each of its values is a **label**. ::: {.diagram} ![The parts of a data table. Each row is one observation; the features are the inputs a model learns from, and the outcome is what it predicts. Rows can share a source: here three rows come from one site.](img/data-table.svg){fig-alt="A table with five rows and the columns site, temperature, salinity, depth and species found. A bracket over temperature, salinity and depth labels them features, the inputs; a bracket over species found labels it the outcome. The first row is highlighted and labelled one row, an observation. A bracket beside the first three rows, all from site A, says site A was visited three times, so they are not three separate observations. A note gives the units: temperature in degrees Celsius, salinity in PSU, depth in metres."} ::: Machine learning grew up in computer science and statistics separately, so each part has several names. The literature uses all of them: | In this course | Also called | What it is | | --- | --- | --- | | **Observation** | row, instance, example, sample, case | One thing that was measured | | **Feature** or **input** | predictor, covariate, independent variable, attribute | Something known about it | | **Outcome** | response, target, dependent variable, $y$ | What the model predicts | | **Label** | class, annotation, ground truth | The outcome when it is a category | Beware of "sample": in machine learning it means one observation, in field science the whole collection. ## One observation is a scientific choice The harder question is what one row should be. A survey that returns to the same sites could have one row for each: - **sample**, as the database stores it; - **visit** to a site, averaging the samples taken that day; - **site**, if the question is about the site's character and not the visit; - **animal**, if the question is about individual growth. The right choice follows from the scientific question, not from how the database stores the data. It matters because a model treats every row as independent evidence. ## The survey returns to the same sites The raw survey file (see [The coastal survey](the-coastal-survey.qmd)) has columns the clean one leaves out. One of them is `site_id`: the survey returns to fixed sites, and each visit to a site is one station. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} raw <- load_coastal_survey_raw() tibble( rows = nrow(raw), `unique rows` = nrow(distinct(raw)), `distinct sites` = n_distinct(raw$site_id) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| rows| unique rows| distinct sites| |----:|-----------:|--------------:| | 815| 800| 160|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} import pandas as pd from mlbasic_data import load_coastal_survey_raw raw = load_coastal_survey_raw() pd.DataFrame({ "rows": [len(raw)], "unique rows": [len(raw.drop_duplicates())], "distinct sites": [raw["site_id"].nunique()], }) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> rows unique rows distinct sites #> 0 815 800 160 ``` ::: ::: ::: The file has 815 rows, 800 once exact duplicates are removed, and only 160 sites. Counting the visits to each site shows why: ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} raw |> distinct() |> count(site_id, name = "visits") |> count(visits, name = "sites") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| visits| sites| |------:|-----:| | 1| 1| | 2| 13| | 3| 24| | 4| 37| | 5| 33| | 6| 16| | 7| 17| | 8| 9| | 9| 6| | 10| 1| | 11| 2| | 15| 1|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} (raw.drop_duplicates()["site_id"] .value_counts() .value_counts() .sort_index() .rename_axis("visits") .reset_index(name="sites")) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> visits sites #> 0 1 1 #> 1 2 13 #> 2 3 24 #> 3 4 37 #> 4 5 33 #> 5 6 16 #> 6 7 17 #> 7 8 9 #> 8 9 6 #> 9 10 1 #> 10 11 2 #> 11 15 1 ``` ::: ::: ::: Most sites, 79%, were visited three to seven times, and one site 15 times. ## Rows that share information A model given this table treats all 815 rows as independent evidence. They are not, in three ways: - **Duplicates.** 15 rows are the same station entered twice. They add no information but count double, and a duplicate can land in the training and the test data at once, where the model predicts it perfectly without having learned anything. That is [information leakage](information-leakage.qmd). - **Repeat visits.** Visits to the same site share the water, the seabed and often the season, so they are closer to repeats of one observation than to separate ones. Ecologists call treating them as separate **pseudo-replication**. - **Nearby sites.** Two sites a few kilometres apart share a water mass and a depth. [Section 6](../06-assumptions-limitations/index.qmd) comes back to this. So the number of independent observations here is nearer 160 than 815, and any score computed as if it were 815 will look better than it should. ## Keep the rows and group them This does not mean throwing rows away: repeat visits show how much a site varies from one visit to the next. The fix is to remove the duplicates and keep each site's rows together when the data is split to test a model, so that a site is never in both the training and the test data. [Splitting the data](splitting-data.qmd) shows how. ## Key points ::: {.key-points} - Each row is an **observation**; the model learns from the **features** (inputs) and predicts the **outcome**. A category outcome's values are **labels**. - What one row represents is a scientific choice, not a database default. - The row count is not the number of independent observations: here 815 rows, 800 unique, 160 sites. - Duplicates, repeat visits and nearby sites all make rows share information. - Keep the rows, but keep each site's rows together when splitting. ::: ## Try it yourself 1. Find the site visited 15 times and look at its rows. How much do they differ, compared with rows from two different sites? 2. For your own data, write one sentence saying what one observation is, and one naming what makes two of your rows share information.
